did_you_know.text: The heading identifies the chapter as a “Psalm of David” intended for the chief musician, and also calls it a “song.”
The verse presents a conceptual tension between silence and praise: even silence before God can be an expression of praise, alongside a commitment to fulfill vows.
The phrase “You who hear prayer” emphasizes God as the one to whom people turn, while “all flesh” gives this appeal a universal character.
The psalm describes iniquities as having overwhelmed people, yet declares that God is also the one who atones for the worshipers’ transgressions.

Blessedness in the chapter is connected with being chosen and drawing near to God: the chosen are described as dwelling in his courts and being satisfied with the goodness of his house and his holy temple.
God is described as one who answers with righteousness and as the security of the ends of the earth and the farthest seas; therefore, his work extends beyond the boundaries of any single place.
In this verse, the sea and its waves represent roaring forces, while “the tumult of the nations” also appears; the psalm thus parallels the stormy forces of nature with human turmoil.
The verses about blessing the land present an agricultural picture: God visits the earth, waters it, enriches it, and prepares the grain to grow.
The image “You crown the year with your goodness” portrays the year as adorned with abundance, while God’s paths are described as overflowing with richness.
At the end of the chapter, all creation joins in the celebration: the pastures, valleys, and hills are filled with vegetation, joyful shouts, and singing.
